newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks falter, but Iraq worries boost dollar.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks falter, but Iraq worries boost dollar.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market's key Nikkei average fell below 20,000 in early morning trade on Tuesday, though brokers said the fall was not due to rising tension in Iraq, which pushed up the dollar against the yen.
The benchmark Nikkei 225 index was battered by newspaper reports of a possible delay in the formation of a supplementary budget for Japan's current fiscal year, brokers said.
The Nikkei slipped as low as 19,920.02, but by midday it was up 88.73 points or 0.44 percent at 20,195.84. Its September futures were up 60 points at 20,210.
"The market had been testing the 20,000 level since yesterday," said Haruo Nakaharu, general manager at Toyo Securities. "There is a small feeling of accomplishment now."

Brokers said the market had been plagued by dark shadows over the domestic economy as well as weakness in Dow industrials late last week, providing the scenario for the Nikkei to sink below 20,000 for the first time since March 15.

Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama told a news conference on Tuesday morning that Tokyo stocks were unlikely to fall drastically and the Japanese government wanted prices to move in a stable manner.
"Stocks remain soft, but I have a feeling (the price decline) will not be very drastic...I want a stable attitude (in the market)," Kajiyama said.
Toyo Securities' Nakaharu said a lack of buy factors would probably mean that the Nikkei would meander near 20,000 for a while.
"After the fall today, the index should be fairly immune to other surprises that events like U.S. payrolls data, due out later this week, may hold," he said.
In the currency market, the dollar was well-bid against the yen by Tuesday midday in Tokyo despite relatively heavy selling by U.S. funds and Japanese exporters at around 109.20-25 yen, dealers said.
Rising tension over the Iraq situation was behind the dollar's solidness, they said.

Commenting on media reports that said airborne U.S. bombers were carrying cruise missiles to an unknown destination, Kajiyama, Japan's top government spokesman, said: "Japan understands that no military action has been taken (against Iraq) as of yet."
Stock market sources said that if the bombers were indeed bound for Iraq, it could develop into a negative factor for stocks.
